title: The Goldfish That Never Forgets
blurb: Everyone says it forgets in three seconds. It remembers for months, it started out gray, and it can survive a frozen pond by turning its own waste into alcohol.

blocks.prompt: The Goldfish That Is Not Really Gold
blocks.text: People say a goldfish forgets everything in three seconds. That is not true. A goldfish can remember for months. It learns the sound of your feet. It learns where the food comes from. It swims to that spot before you even open the lid. A goldfish is not born gold. Long ago, all of them were gray. People in China found a few orange ones and kept them safe in ponds. Those orange fish had orange babies. After many years, the ponds were full of gold. Every goldfish you see today came from those gray fish.

3.title: The Goldfish That Never Forgets
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: The three second memory is a myth

blocks.prompt: The Three Second Myth
blocks.text: You have probably heard that a goldfish has a memory of three seconds. It is one of the most repeated facts in the world, and it is wrong. Scientists have tested it. They taught goldfish to push a small lever to get food. The fish learned it. Then the scientists made the lever work for only one hour each day. Within a week, the goldfish were crowding around the lever at the right hour and ignoring it the rest of the time. That is not a three second memory. That is a fish reading a clock. Other tests have gone further. Goldfish have learned to swim through mazes, to tell one color from another, and to pick out one sound and ignore another. Some have even been trained to drive. Researchers put a goldfish tank on wheels with a camera above it, and the fish learned to steer the tank across a room toward a target. Nobody knows exactly where the three second story started. It has been passed along for so long that most people never think to check it.

answers: a small lever that gave them food
the fish showed up at the lever at the right hour and ignored it the rest of the time
swim through mazes, tell colors apart, tell sounds apart, or steer a tank on wheels
(inference: it gets repeated so often that nobody stops to check it)

4.title: The Goldfish That Never Forgets
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A goldfish is a carp, bred by people for about a thousand years
Its wild ancestor is silver gray
Selective breeding made the fantail, the oranda, the telescope eye
In a pond it can pass a foot long
A healthy goldfish can live twenty years or more
Bowls hold too little water and too little oxygen

blocks.prompt: From Gray Carp to Gold
blocks.text: A goldfish is a carp with a thousand years of human decisions behind it. Its ancestor is a plain silver gray carp that still swims in rivers across Asia. Nothing about it looks remarkable. Now and then, though, one of those carp hatched with a mistake in its color and came out orange or yellow instead of gray. In a river, that mistake is close to a death sentence. A bright fish in dull water is easy for a heron to spot. About a thousand years ago, in China, people began lifting those bright fish out of the rivers and moving them into ponds where nothing could eat them. In the pond, the mistake became an advantage. Orange fish were kept and bred. Gray fish were not. Generation after generation, the ponds grew brighter. This is the same process that turned wolves into poodles, and it produced the same kind of variety. Breeders chose for wide flowing tails, for round egg shaped bodies, for eyes that bulge out sideways, and for eyes that point straight up at the sky. A slim comet goldfish and a lumpy oranda are the same species, shaped by different human choices. There is one decision people got badly wrong. The glass bowl. A bowl holds very little water, and its narrow opening lets almost no oxygen in. A healthy goldfish is not a small fish. In a pond it can pass a foot in length and live for twenty years or more. A goldfish in a bowl usually stays small and dies young, and people mistake that for how goldfish simply are. The fish was never built for the bowl. The bowl was built for us, because it is easy to look through.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.
items: Why was being orange dangerous for a carp in a river?
Explain how a pond flipped that danger into an advantage.
The passage compares goldfish breeding to wolves becoming poodles. What is the point of that comparison?
The author says the bowl was built for us. What does that suggest about how people chose to keep goldfish?
answers: a bright fish is easy for a predator like a heron to see in dull water
in a pond nothing could eat the bright fish, so people could keep and breed the orange ones
(both are selective breeding: people choosing which animals reproduce until the whole population changes)
(inference: the bowl suits the owner's view, not the fish's needs)

blocks.prompt: Circle the main idea of this passage.

answers: The goldfish is a wild carp reshaped by a thousand years of human choices, including one bad choice

5.title: The Goldfish That Never Forgets
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Carassius auratus, a domesticated carp
Released goldfish can pass fourteen inches and weigh pounds
They feed by rooting through the bottom mud
Tracked goldfish in Australia traveled over a hundred miles
One female can carry tens of thousands of eggs
They tolerate warm, dirty, low oxygen water

blocks.prompt: The Fish You Should Not Set Free
blocks.text: Every few years the same photograph goes around. Someone stands at the edge of a lake holding a goldfish the size of a dinner plate. It is orange, unmistakable, and far too large. The photograph is not a hoax. It is what happens when a pet goldfish is let go. Inside a bowl or a small tank, a goldfish stays small, and people assume that is its natural size. It is not. Growth in fish is held back by cramped space, by poor water quality, and by chemicals the fish itself releases into water that is not changed often enough. Remove those limits and the animal keeps going. In an open lake, with room and food and years, a goldfish can pass fourteen inches and weigh several pounds. Crews netting lakes in Minnesota have pulled out goldfish by the tens of thousands. In Australia, researchers tagged released goldfish and tracked them traveling more than a hundred miles through a river system. The size is not really the problem. Goldfish feed by rooting through the bottom, sucking up mud and spitting out whatever they do not want. In a garden pond that is harmless. In a lake, thousands of them stir the sediment up into the water until sunlight can no longer reach the plants below. The plants die. The water clouds and turns green with algae. Goldfish also eat the eggs of native fish and the insects those fish depend on, and they tolerate warm, dirty, low oxygen water that would kill their competitors. They inherit the lake by outlasting everyone else in it. They are miserably hard to remove. A single female can carry tens of thousands of eggs, and goldfish will breed with wild carp. Once a population takes hold, the tools left are nets, traps, and in the worst cases poisoning the entire lake and starting over. None of this is the fish's fault. A goldfish in a lake is only doing what a carp does. The mistake belongs to the person standing on the bank, who wanted to do something kind and did not know that the kind thing was a door out of a life the fish could never have left on its own.

6.title: The Goldfish That Never Forgets
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Carassius auratus, cousin of the crucian carp
Survives months in water with no oxygen at all
Converts lactic acid into ethanol and breathes it out through the gills
Blood alcohol measured above 50 mg per 100 mL
The trick came from a whole genome duplication about 8 million years ago
Stores fuel in an unusually large liver

blocks.prompt: The Fish That Drinks Its Way Through Winter
blocks.text: Somewhere under the ice of a frozen pond in northern Europe, a fish is quietly drunk, and that is the only reason it is still alive. When a pond freezes over, the lid closes. Ice cuts the water off from the air, and whatever oxygen is still dissolved down there gets used up by everything living in it. Within weeks the pond is anoxic, meaning it holds essentially no oxygen at all. For nearly every vertebrate on Earth, that is fatal in minutes. Brains are expensive to run. Deprived of oxygen, a human brain starts dying in about four minutes. The goldfish, and its wild cousin the crucian carp, can sit in that black airless water for months and swim out in spring. Here is how. Cells normally burn sugar using oxygen, which is efficient and clean. When the oxygen runs out, cells fall back on anaerobic glycolysis, a backup that yields far less energy and leaves lactic acid behind. That is the burn in your legs at the end of a sprint. The backup buys minutes, not months, because the acid piles up and eventually poisons the very tissue producing it. Every animal that runs out of oxygen runs into this same wall. The goldfish walks around the wall. Its muscle carries a second set of enzymes that most fish simply do not have. When oxygen disappears, those enzymes take the same waste product and, rather than stopping at lactic acid, carry the reaction two steps further and convert it into ethanol. Ethanol is alcohol, and an alcohol molecule is small enough to slip out of the blood, cross the gill membrane, and drift away into the pond. The poison leaves the building. The fish keeps going. The chemistry is not free. Producing ethanol wastes fuel, so the fish slows everything it can: it barely moves, its heart rate falls, and its brain drops into a low energy mode. It lives off sugar packed into an unusually large liver. And it really does get drunk on the way. Measurements have put the blood alcohol of an anoxic crucian carp above 50 milligrams per 100 milliliters, which is over the legal driving limit in a good number of countries. Where did that second set of enzymes come from? Roughly eight million years ago, an ancestor of these fish duplicated its entire genome. A duplication like that leaves a spare copy of every gene, and spare copies are free to drift, because the original is still doing the job. One spare wandered into a new function, and a lineage of carp bought itself an entire season that no competitor could survive. That is the whole trick. Not strength, not speed, not intelligence. Just the ability to still be there in March when everything else is gone. This is the animal we use as shorthand for stupidity. The three second memory is a myth, comfortably disproved decades ago. So is the assumption underneath it, that a goldfish is a simple thing. A goldfish in a bowl is not a simple animal in its natural state. It is a survivor of ice age ponds, parked in a glass jar in a warm room, with nothing left to survive.

answers: (original one-sentence summary: a common pet fish survives oxygen free winters by turning its own waste into alcohol and releasing it, thanks to a duplicated genome)
the acid accumulates and kills the tissue making it; quote: the acid piles up and eventually poisons the very tissue producing it
(it converts lactic acid into ethanol; a small molecule can cross the gill membrane and leave into the pond, so the waste is removed instead of stored)
(it strips away the qualities we admire and reframes survival as persistence, setting up the closing argument that we misjudge the fish)
(it argues the bowl removes the challenge the animal was built for; earned by the winter evidence, though the reader has to accept the value judgment)
